Reference

The public API of IDTrack, module by module. The most used names are also importable from idtrack itself (idtrack.API, idtrack.ConversionResult, the errors, …); they are documented here under the module that holds them. Modules and names without a leading underscore are public.

The API

The public API of idtrack: load (or build) a graph, convert identifiers, describe the graph, look up names.

An API holds one loaded graph (one organism, one snapshot release) and nothing else that changes between calls: every conversion is a function of its arguments and the graph, every result is a frozen dataclass of idtrack.results with a strict-JSON to_dict(), and every argument is checked once, here, before any search starts. A wrong argument raises an idtrack.errors.InputError that names it and the accepted values; nothing else is the caller’s fault.

Loading a graph file (API.load()) reads that one file and nothing else: no network, no table, and none of the build stack (pandas, h5py, PyMySQL, PyYAML) is imported. Building (API.build()) is its own call.

Conversions only read the graph, so several threads may convert at once with the same answers as one; the search holds the interpreter lock, so a server scales with processes, not threads.

class API(graph, *, search=None)[source]

Bases: object

The public interface of idtrack over one loaded graph.

Make one with load() (a graph file), build() (from Ensembl, or the file of the same graph in a local repository) or API(graph) (a graph in memory).

graph

The graph.

Type:

TheGraph

engine

The conversion engine over the graph.

Type:

Track

Hold a graph.

Parameters:

  • graph (TheGraph) – The graph (idtrack.graph.TheGraph.load(), or built by idtrack.build.GraphMaker).

  • search (SearchSettings | None) – The default search settings; None for the defaults of idtrack.settings.SearchSettings.

Raises:

ArgumentTypeError – If graph is not a idtrack.graph.TheGraph, or search not a idtrack.settings.SearchSettings.

classmethod build(organism, snapshot_release, local_repository, *, first_release=None, rebuild=False, search=None, graph_settings=None)[source]

Build the graph of an organism and snapshot release from Ensembl’s tables, and load it.

The graph holds every release from first_release to snapshot_release, on the organism’s assemblies in their order of the organism table; its primary assembly is the preferred one that has snapshot_release. Tables already in local_repository are not downloaded again. If the repository holds the file of this graph (graph_path()), and it is the graph asked for (the same selection of external databases and organism table), it is loaded instead of built, unless rebuild; a file of another graph under the same name is an error (idtrack.errors.GraphMismatchError), never silently replaced.

Parameters:

  • organism (str) – The organism.

  • snapshot_release (int) – The last release of the graph; later releases are ignored.

  • local_repository (str) – An existing folder for the tables and the graph file.

  • first_release (int | None) – The first release of the window; None: the organism’s first release.

  • rebuild (bool) – Build even if the file exists, and replace it.

  • search (SearchSettings | None) – The default search settings of the API.

  • graph_settings (GraphSettings | None) – The caches and hyper-connectivity threshold of the graph.

Returns:

An API over the graph.

Return type:

API

Raises:

  • idtrack.errors.InputError – For an unknown organism, release or assembly, or a folder that does not exist.

  • idtrack.errors.GraphMismatchError – If the file holds another graph than the one asked for.

  • idtrack.errors.BuildError – If Ensembl cannot be reached or its tables cannot be built into a graph.

static classify(results, strategy='best')[source]

Group conversion results into bins for reporting, by the targets of one view (best or all).

Every result is in "input_identifiers" and in exactly one of the bins "matching_1_to_0" (not found, no conversion, or an error), "read_at_another_release" (a result with candidates that the graph could not read at the release given, read where it holds the identifier: an answer to another question, idtrack.results.ConversionResult.from_release_fallback), "matching_1_to_1", "matching_1_to_n", "alternative_target_1_to_1" and "alternative_target_1_to_n" (the last two: no_target, the targets are Ensembl genes standing in for a missing id of the requested database). A result of "matching_1_to_1" is also in "changed_only_1_to_1" when its target is not the identifier it resolved to, and one of "matching_1_to_n" is also in "changed_only_1_to_n" when none of its targets is. “The identifier it resolved to” is graph_id, compared without the graph’s synonym prefix and, for Ensembl ids, without the version (idtrack.ids.stable_id_of()), so that a query without version or in another case that maps to itself is not “changed”.

Parameters:

  • results (list[ConversionResult]) – Results of convert_many() or convert().

  • strategy (str) – "best" or "all": which view’s targets count.

The bins (BINS).

dict[str, list[ConversionResult]]

convert(identifier, from_release=None, to_release=None, final_database=None, *, from_database=None, explain=False, allow_bridges=True, budget_states=None, budget_seconds=None)[source]

Convert one identifier to a target release and database: every candidate, ranked, the best marked.

The identifier is resolved to a node of the graph (idtrack.graph.TheGraph.resolve_name()): between the nodes the string can mean, one that exists at from_release (without one: at to_release, or, where none exists there, at the latest release at which one does; one release decides both the node and where it is read) is taken before one that does not (with from_database: as an id of that database), and an Ensembl id is never passed over. Among those it is matched exactly (as a database wrote the identifier at the release it is read at), then ignoring letter case, then taking -, _ and . as one character, then without the version of a sequence accession, each step on names and then on synonyms before the next begins. How it matched is reported (idtrack.results.ConversionResult.match). The engine (idtrack.engine.Track.convert()) then finds its Ensembl gene(s) at to_release and their ids in final_database, ranks them and marks the best answer: result.view("best") and result.view("all") are the two views of the one search.

Parameters:

  • identifier (str) – Ensembl id (with or without version), symbol or other external id. Surrounding white space is ignored.

  • from_release (int | None) – Ensembl release at which identifier is read. If None, it is read at to_release when it is active there, otherwise at the latest release in which it is active. If a release is given at which the graph does not hold the identifier, the identifier is read by the same rule as without from_release, and the result says so (from_release_fallback, and reasons holds "read_at_another_release", the reason of a result with targets: an answer to what the identifier meant where it was read).

  • to_release (int | None) – Target Ensembl release; None means the graph’s snapshot release.

  • final_database (str | None) – Database of the targets (final_databases() of to_release, matched case-insensitively); None means "ensembl_gene".

  • from_database (str | None) – The external database identifier is meant as (one of external_databases()); None reads it in any database.

  • explain (bool) – Add idtrack.results.ConversionResult.path, the paths of the candidates as data (no step when there is no candidate), with every bridge the search considered and the rule that took or refused it.

  • allow_bridges (bool) – Allow bridges through ids two genes share when the history leads to no gene (only where the bridge is evidence that one gene became the other: idtrack.engine.track.Track.convert()).

  • budget_states (int | None) – The search budget of this call in states (default: search).

  • budget_seconds (float | None) – The search budget of this call in seconds (default: search).

Returns:

The result.

Return type:

ConversionResult

Raises:

  • idtrack.errors.InputError – For an argument that is not valid (the subclass names which).

  • idtrack.errors.SearchBudgetExceededError – If the search needs more than its budget.

convert_many(identifiers, from_release=None, to_release=None, final_database=None, *, from_database=None, explain=False, allow_bridges=True, budget_states=None, budget_seconds=None, progress=False)[source]

Convert a batch of identifiers with the same arguments; one identifier’s error never stops the batch.

The arguments are checked once, before any conversion: a batch that is not a sequence of strings raises with the positions of the items that are neither strings nor missing values, as do invalid releases or databases. Each item is read as convert() reads its identifier; an item that is refused there (an empty string or a spelling of a missing value: idtrack.errors.MissingValueError; a string longer than any identifier or one of the graph’s internal names: idtrack.errors.InvalidArgumentError), an item that is a missing value as Python, NumPy or pandas hold it (None, NaN, pd.NA, NaT: what a column of a table holds in an empty cell; a idtrack.errors.MissingValueError, its query_id the value written as text) and any other error of one identifier (an exceeded budget, an internal error) is that item’s idtrack.results.ConversionResult.error, with status error, and the batch goes on. Each distinct identifier is converted once; repeated identifiers get the same (immutable) result. An item is answered as convert() answers it alone, but for the copies of decision 82 (below).

Parameters:

  • identifiers (Iterable[str]) – The identifiers (a list, tuple, NumPy array, pandas Index or Series of strings, which may hold missing values; not a str).

  • from_release (int | None) – See convert().

  • to_release (int | None) – See convert().

  • final_database (str | None) – See convert().

  • from_database (str | None) – See convert().

  • explain (bool) – See convert().

  • allow_bridges (bool) – See convert().

  • budget_states (int | None) – See convert() (per identifier).

  • budget_seconds (float | None) – See convert() (per identifier).

  • progress (bool) – Show a progress bar on the console.

Returns:

One result per input identifier, in input order.

Return type:

list[ConversionResult]

Raises:

idtrack.errors.InputError – For a batch or an argument that is not valid.

source_inference(identifiers, mode='assembly_release')[source]

Infer where a list of identifiers comes from: the origins it cannot tell apart, and by how much.

Each distinct identifier counts once (decision 97) for every origin (database, assembly, release) at which it is an identifier, read as it is at that release (decision 79): a string counts at a release where name resolution at that release (idtrack.graph.TheGraph.readings()) reads it as a name of that release, so that a name renamed later counts as the name it was where it was one, and not at the releases where it is only a synonym (a synonym says the string was once a name or an alias, not that a table of that release wrote it). An Ensembl id counts at every origin of its node (idtrack.graph.TheGraph.trios()). Strings refused as identifiers (missing values, the graph’s internal names), missing values as a table holds them (None, NaN, pd.NA, NaT) and strings not in the graph are counted in SourceInference.not_found.

The best origin is the one where most identifiers are found. Another origin belongs to the band of origins the list cannot tell apart from the best unless the identifiers found at one of the two and not at the other make it significantly worse: a one-sided sign test on those identifiers at the level SOURCE_SIGNIFICANCE (a list of the names of release R is found whole at R, and its neighbours lose only the few names renamed between them). The margin is the best count minus the count of the best origin outside the band.

Parameters:

  • identifiers (Iterable[str]) – Identifiers (a sequence of strings, which may hold missing values; not a str).

  • mode (str) – Granularity of an origin (idtrack.engine.SOURCE_MODES): "complete" → [database, assembly, release], "release" → release, "assembly" → assembly, "assembly_release" (default) → [assembly, release].

Returns:

The band, the margin and the count of every origin.

Return type:

SourceInference

Raises:

  • idtrack.errors.InvalidArgumentError – If mode is unknown.

  • idtrack.errors.ArgumentTypeError – If identifiers is not a sequence of strings.

  • idtrack.errors.UnknownIdentifierError – If none of the identifiers is in the graph.

BINS = ('changed_only_1_to_n', 'changed_only_1_to_1', 'alternative_target_1_to_1', 'alternative_target_1_to_n', 'matching_1_to_0', 'matching_1_to_1', 'matching_1_to_n', 'read_at_another_release', 'input_identifiers')

The bins of API.classify().

SOURCE_SIGNIFICANCE = 0.05

The level of the sign test that tells the origins of a list apart (API.source_inference()).

Results

The typed results of idtrack’s public calls: frozen dataclasses with a lossless, strict-JSON to_dict().

Every result is plain data: strings, integers, floats (never NaN or infinity: a missing number is None), booleans, None, tuples and nested results. to_dict() turns a result into dict/list/scalars that json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False) writes, and from_dict() reads it back into an equal result.

  • ConversionResult: one identifier converted (idtrack.API.convert()). Its candidates are every target the search reached, ranked, the best marked (Candidate.best); best and all are two views of the one search (ConversionResult.view()). decided_by names the criterion that put the best answer before the runner-up, and status with reason says why a result has no target.

  • ExplainedPath: the path of every candidate as data, one graph per conversion (nodes and steps), with every bridge the search considered and the rule that took or refused it (BridgeCheck).

  • GraphDescription: what a loaded graph holds, without the network.

  • NameMatch: a name of an external database attached to a gene at releases.

This module imports only idtrack.errors.

A bridge the search considered from one gene to another, and the rule that took or refused it.

The search considers bridges only where Ensembl’s history leads to no gene at the target release, from every gene the history reached, and only those it can place in time (the far side holds at a release between the near side’s and the target release); every such pair of genes is listed once.

It holds for the string as typed (decision 102): where the string has letters of both cases, only a display name that its database spelt so; a string in one letter case carries no evidence of case and is read without it. How the identifier is the display name of an entry gene, as the ranking compares it: 0 the display name (for a string in one letter case in an organism whose symbols are written in mixed case, the display name of a name authority, read without letter case); 1 for such a string, the display name of another source; 2 not its display name (display_name is False only then).

Type:

int

entry_support

The number of databases that attach the identifier to an entry gene at the starting release (1 for an Ensembl id). For an identifier of digits only, databases of other numbers (an NCBI gene id and a Havana number spelt alike) are not counted against each other: their genes tie (decision 86).

int

own_version

The gene is the queried gene id’s own version at the target release (an id that exists at the target release is its own answer).

bool

final_confidence

0: the target is attached to the gene at the target release; 1: attached to a transcript or translation that belonged to the gene at another release; None: no gene has an id in the requested database and the gene itself is the target.

int | None

bridges

The bridges through external ids (or shared transcripts) on the path; 0 is Ensembl’s history alone.

int

bridge_gap

The releases between leaving a gene and entering the next, summed over the bridges.

int

score

The product of Ensembl’s mapping scores along the history of the path (1.0 without a scored event).

float

unscored_steps

The history steps of the path between two different ids that Ensembl gave no score (it writes 0 where it measured nothing); a path with such a step ranks below every path whose scores are measured, before score compares them (decision 57).

int

same_as_query

The target is the identifier itself (or the gene id it was read as).

Type:

bool

external_steps

Cross-reference edges on the path.

Type:

int

history_steps

History edges on the path.

Type:

int

annotation

(-external ids, -transcripts, -translations) of the gene at the target release, where the engine compared it (between successors of one entry gene that are equal in everything else); None where it did not.

Type:

tuple[int, …] | None

path

With explain: the indices of ExplainedPath.steps from the identifier to gene, in order; empty otherwise.

tuple[int, …]

With explain: the indices of the steps from gene to target (empty when the gene is the target).

Type:

tuple[int, …]

MATCH_PREFIXES: dict[str, str] = {'copy': "In a batch: a name made unique by a single-cell tool (another item of the batch with -1, .1 or _1 appended, itself no exact name at the release it is read at alone); the result is that item's (decision 82).", 'lrg': "An LRG record's id, answered with the gene the record describes (decision 96).", 'par_y': "GENCODE's form of the Y copy of a pseudoautosomal gene (<id>_PAR_Y) was read as the gene's id; the Y copy is reported apart (decision 93).", 'punctuation': 'Stray punctuation was removed before matching: quotes around the identifier, a trailing semicolon, comma or full stop (decision 83).', 'synonym': 'A synonym that a database records for the gene, not the name the database gives it.', 'unicode': 'Unicode was normalised before matching: invisible and control characters (zero-width characters, byte-order marks, bidirectional marks, soft hyphens) removed, compatibility forms (NFKC: full-width letters and digits) and Unicode dashes read as their plain characters (decision 84).'}

What else a match says, as prefixes of ConversionResult.match in this order.

MATCH_STEPS: dict[str, str] = {'case': 'The identifier when letter case is ignored.', 'exact': 'The identifier as written (for an external identifier: as a database wrote it at the release read).', 'separator': "The identifier when '-', '_' and '.' are taken as one character (and letter case is ignored).", 'version': "A sequence accession with the version written after it, read where Ensembl's cross references attached that version.", 'version_newer_than_graph': "An Ensembl id or a sequence accession with a version newer than every version the graph holds, read as its latest version (an id active, an accession attached, at the graph's last release).", 'version_not_judged': "A sequence accession with a version that is not judged: Ensembl's records hold only an edit counter of the records of its database (UniProt's entry version), so the accession is read without it."}

the steps of name resolution (idtrack.graph.TheGraph.resolve_name()). A match is one step, after the prefixes of MATCH_PREFIXES that apply, each followed by : ("unicode:punctuation:synonym:exact").

Type:

How an identifier matched the graph node it was read as (ConversionResult.match)

PLACE_RELATIONS: dict[str, str] = {'no_place': 'The graph holds no place for one of the two genes.', 'other_assemblies': 'The two genes never lie on one assembly at the same time, and nothing tells them apart (a sequence of one name, or a scaffold): their places cannot be compared.', 'outside_reference': "A gene lies outside the reference sequence (a patch, a haplotype, an alternative locus, an LRG record), and nothing places it apart from the other gene (it lies inside its assembly exception's reference region, or it is an LRG record, which has none): its place is not compared base by base with the reference sequence.", 'places_apart': "On one assembly the two genes do not overlap: another sequence region, another strand, or apart; or a place carried onto the other's assembly by Ensembl's mapping of the two assemblies shares no base with it; or a copy's reference region (Ensembl's assembly exception) shares no base with the other gene; or, on two assemblies that no published mapping joins, they lie on chromosomes of different names (the mitochondrial genome against a chromosome among them), which no assembly change turns one into the other.", 'same_place': "On one assembly the two genes overlap (one sequence region, one strand), or a place carried onto the other's assembly by Ensembl's mapping of the two assemblies overlaps it."}

Where two genes lie relative to each other (BridgeCheck.places and PathStep.places), from the places the graph holds (idtrack.TheGraph.places()). Two places are compared base by base on one assembly and on its reference sequence (they overlap when they share a base on one sequence region and one strand), and across an assembly change where Ensembl’s mapping of the two assemblies carries the earlier place onto the later assembly; a copy on a patch or haplotype is compared by the reference region its assembly exception replaces; across assemblies otherwise, two genes that lie on chromosomes or the mitochondrial genome only, on sequences of different names, lie apart (idtrack.graph.genes.relation()).

identity (the gene is its own answer), entry (from the identifier to the gene it stands for), history (an event of Ensembl’s id history), self_loop (a scored re-mapping of a gene to itself), bridge_near and bridge_far (the two sides of a bridge through an id two genes carry), final (from the gene to its id in the final database).

old_release

For a history step: the old side of Ensembl’s event, the last release of the event’s earlier id. Ensembl’s events run forward in time, the walk may not: walking forward the earlier id is source, walking backward (to an earlier target release) it is target.

new_release

For a history step: the new side of the event, the first release of the event’s later id (target walking forward, source walking backward).

int

merges

int

databases

int | None

old_assembly

int | None

reason

Why the step was taken (or, for a step of ExplainedPath.refused, why it was not): a key of STEP_REASONS.

str

READING_REASONS: dict[str, str] = {'make_unique_suffix': 'The string ends in a suffix that single-cell tools append to make names unique (-1, .1, _1); reading it, with its separators taken as one or without letter case, as a synonym of another gene than the string before the suffix names is not taken (decision 82).', 'other_release': 'The string means this identifier at other releases only (the releases listed), not at the release it was read at: what it meant at another time (a name of one gene then, a synonym of another gene now). Give from_release to read it there.', 'same_step': 'The step that matched reached this identifier as well, at the same release (decision 87); its candidates are part of the answer, ranked with those of the reading taken by the same evidence of lineage.', 'symbol_without_case': 'In an organism whose symbols follow a letter-case convention, a string written otherwise that is not exactly a name is read first as a symbol of the organism without letter case, where that names exactly one gene (decisions 55 and 80); this reading came after it.', 'unversioned_database': "The string is an identifier followed by a version, and the identifier is, at the release read, also an id of a database that writes its ids without a version (an NCBI gene id spelt like a numeric Havana id of the early releases): where no database has the identifier with that version at that release, the string has two readings, and this is the other one (the identifier as that database's id, without the suffix)."}

Why a reading of an identifier is reported beside the one taken (OtherReading.reason).

REASONS: dict[str, str] = {'error': 'The conversion of this identifier raised an error (see `error`).', 'never_active': 'The identifier is never active on the assemblies that serve the releases of this graph.', 'no_gene_at_start': 'At the release it is read at, the identifier is attached to no gene.', 'no_id_in_final_database': 'The genes reached have no id in the requested database.', 'no_path_to_target': "Ensembl's history (and the bridges allowed) leads to no gene at the target release.", 'not_an_id_of_database': 'The identifier is an Ensembl id, not an id of the database named as its source.', 'not_in_graph': 'The identifier is not an identifier of this graph at any release.', 'read_at_another_release': 'The graph does not hold the identifier at the release given (`from_release_given`); it was read where the graph holds it (`from_release`), so the targets are what the identifier meant there, which can be another gene than the one it meant at the release given.', 'unknown_version': 'The identifier is an Ensembl id, or a sequence accession, with a version this graph does not hold.', 'version_not_judged': "The version written after the accession was not judged: Ensembl's records hold only an edit counter of the records of its database, not a version of the sequence; the accession was read without it."}

Why a conversion has no target in the requested database, or answers another question than the one asked (ConversionResult.reason).

Errors

The errors of idtrack, in one hierarchy rooted in IdtrackError.

A caller (a script, a notebook, a web server) can tell from the class alone whose fault an error is:

  • InputError: the caller asked for something the package or the loaded graph does not have, or passed an argument of the wrong kind. The subclasses name the argument: an unknown organism, release, assembly, database or identifier, a missing value, an Ensembl id at a release where it is not active or with a version that does not exist, an argument of the wrong type or value. Each subclass also derives from the built-in error that it replaces (ValueError, or TypeError for a value of the wrong type), so except ValueError keeps working.

  • GraphFileError: a graph file is missing, unreadable, of another format, or holds another graph than the one asked for (GraphMismatchError).

  • SearchBudgetExceededError: one conversion needed more work than its budget; an outcome of that one identifier, which a batch records and goes on.

  • BuildError: building tables or a graph failed: Ensembl could not be reached or answered something unusable (EnsemblAccessError, also a ConnectionError), a table or a schema is not what the builder needs, the history does not validate, the externals configuration does not cover a release.

  • IntegrityError: the package or a graph contradicts itself; a bug or a damaged file, never the caller’s input.

This module imports nothing of idtrack.

exception EnsemblSchemaError(message, table, missing_columns=())[source]

Bases: BuildError, LookupError

An Ensembl core database has no such table, or the table lacks requested columns.

It states a fact about the schema of one release (older releases keep stable ids in <form>_stable_id tables, and some columns were renamed), so callers may fall back to the older layout when they catch it. A failed download, a connection error or a failure to cache a table never raises it; those keep their own exception, so that a fallback cannot hide them.

Settings

Settings of idtrack: how Ensembl is reached (for building), how a search is bounded, and how a graph is cached.

Three kinds, each one object:

  • SearchSettings (frozen): the budget of one conversion and the rules of bridges. An idtrack.API holds one (API.load(path, search=...)), and every conversion call can override the budget for itself (budget_states, budget_seconds). Nothing of it is process-wide.

  • GraphSettings (frozen): the hyper-connectivity threshold and the bounds of the per-node caches of one loaded graph (API.load(path, graph_settings=...), idtrack.graph.TheGraph.load()).

  • ENSEMBL (EnsemblSettings): hosts, timeouts, retries and the access mode of the build stack (MySQL or Ensembl’s HTTPS dumps, and Ensembl REST). Network settings are a property of the process: set them once at start with configure_ensembl(), which checks every value. A loaded graph never uses the network.

This module imports only idtrack.errors.

ACCESS_MODES: tuple[str, ...] = ('auto', 'https')

VERSION_EDIT_COUNTER_SHARE = 0.5

The share of the pairs of consecutive releases of one link (an accession, one version of an Ensembl id, a database) in which the version that Ensembl’s cross reference gives the accession differs, above which a database’s number is an edit counter of its records and not a version of the sequence (decision 101; idtrack.graph.TheGraph.edit_counter_databases()): a version of the sequence holds while the link holds, so that “the releases at which the accession had that version” are a stretch of time; a number that changes with nearly every release (UniProt’s entry version, Q9TSV4.120) identifies no state that a typed version could mean. Measured on the five graphs of Ensembl 115: RefSeq, CCDS, Havana and Vega 0 to 3.8 % of the pairs (human’s Havana translations 14.6 %), UniProt’s Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL 58 to 99.7 % (docs/usage.rst); one half lies in the gap between the two.

Organisms

The organisms idtrack knows: their genome assemblies, release ranges and order, symbol databases and short names.

The one table of organisms is ORGANISM_TABLE ({organism: {assembly key: entry}}); change it only with register_organism(), which validates the whole table first and recomputes what is derived from it. The functions of this module answer questions about it (the first release of an organism, its assemblies by priority, the assembly that serves a release) without the network, and resolve_organism() turns an organism’s name or short name into the name of the table.

This module imports only idtrack.errors, idtrack.ids and idtrack.settings.

ALIASES: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]] = {'homo_sapiens': ('human',), 'macaca_fascicularis': ('cynomolgus',), 'macaca_mulatta': ('rhesus',), 'mus_musculus': ('mouse',), 'sus_scrofa': ('pig',)}

Short names of the organisms. A declared alias names its organism wherever an organism is asked for, without the network, and wins over what Ensembl lists under the same word ("pig" is the common name of every pig breed there). Lower case, unique across organisms.

The label under which a graph reports the Ensembl ids of each form on each assembly key, {assembly: {form: "assembly_<key>_ensembl_<form>"}}: the source of an Ensembl id on an assembly in idtrack.TheGraph.trios() and idtrack.TheGraph.combined(), in the inference of the source of a list, and in the self-checks (derived from the table; updated in place by register_organism()).

NCBI_GENE_DATABASE = 'EntrezGene'

Ensembl’s name of NCBI Gene’s database (external_db.db_name, the same at every release). Its accessions are the NCBI gene numbers, its label rows NCBI’s official symbols, which a graph names by the rule of decision 53 (the name Ensembl’s tables give them: idtrack.TheGraph.label_names); NCBI’s symbols are the symbols of a name authority beside SYMBOL_DATABASES (idtrack.TheGraph.authority_databases, decision 94).

PSEUDOAUTOSOMAL_REGIONS: dict[str, tuple[tuple[tuple[str, int, int], tuple[str, int, int]], ...]] = {'GRCh38': ((('Y', 10001, 2781479), ('X', 10001, 2781479)), (('Y', 56887903, 57217415), ('X', 155701383, 156030895)))}

pairs of a region of Y and the region of X that it repeats, ((region, first base, last base), (region, first base, last base)) (the Genome Reference Consortium’s PAR1 and PAR2 of GRCh38). From release 110 Ensembl gives the Y copies of the genes of these regions ids of their own (decisions 93 and 95). Ensembl records the same regions in its core databases as assembly exceptions of the type PAR (table assembly_exception), which a built graph holds since the builder reads the exceptions for the copies on patches and haplotypes (idtrack.TheGraph.assembly_exceptions; GRCh38’s two PAR rows equal this table); the rule of the Y copies still reads this table, which also serves graphs made in memory. It holds only the assembly whose Y copies have ids of their own.

Type:

The pseudoautosomal regions of an assembly, by Ensembl’s name of the assembly

SYMBOL_DATABASES: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]] = {'homo_sapiens': ('HGNC Symbol',), 'macaca_fascicularis': ('VGNC Symbol', 'HGNC Symbol'), 'macaca_mulatta': ('VGNC Symbol', 'HGNC Symbol'), 'mus_musculus': ('MGI Symbol',), 'sus_scrofa': ('VGNC Symbol', 'HGNC Symbol')}

register_organism(name, assemblies, symbol_databases=None, aliases=None)[source]

Add an organism to the organism table, or replace its entry, and recompute what is derived from the table.

This is the supported way to try an organism that idtrack does not declare (or to change a declared one) within a Python session; to make it permanent, add the same entry to ORGANISM_TABLE in idtrack/organisms.py. The whole table is validated before anything changes, so a rejected entry leaves the table as it was. The table, SYMBOL_DATABASES and the derived values are updated in place, so references to them taken earlier stay current.

Example

>>> from idtrack import organisms
>>> organisms.register_organism(
...     "danio_rerio",
...     {11: {"Name": "GRCz11", "Ports": [3306, 5306], "Priority": 1, "ReleaseRange": [92, None]}},
...     symbol_databases=["ZFIN"],
... )
Parameters:

  • name (str) – Ensembl production name of the organism (e.g. "danio_rerio").

  • assemblies (Mapping[int, Mapping[str, Any]]) – {assembly key: entry} with the fields described in the comment block of ORGANISM_TABLE.

  • symbol_databases (Sequence[str] | None) – Ordered gene-symbol databases of the organism (names as in its externals YAML). Required for a new organism (an empty list if it has none, in which case idtrack.harmonize.HarmonizeFeatures needs an explicit final_database). When an organism already in the table is replaced and this is omitted (None), its current symbol databases are kept.

  • aliases (Sequence[str] | None) – Short names of the organism (lower case, e.g. ["zebrafish"]), which then resolve to it wherever an organism is asked for. None keeps the aliases of an organism that is replaced and gives a new organism none.

Raises:

InvalidArgumentError – If symbol_databases is omitted for a new organism, or if the resulting table violates a rule of the table.

Return type:

None

The graph’s vocabulary

The vocabulary of idtrack’s graph and the one rule of Ensembl ids with versions (<id>.<version>).

Node types, the marks of a gene id’s birth and retirement (<id>.Void, <id>.Retired), the prefix under which the graph keeps synonyms, and the functions that join and split an Ensembl id and its version. Every module that needs one of these takes it from here.

This module imports nothing of idtrack except idtrack.errors.

BACKBONE_FORM = 'gene'

The form whose history is the backbone of the graph.

BASE_ENSEMBL_TYPE = mappingproxy({'gene': 'base_ensembl_gene', 'transcript': 'base_ensembl_transcript', 'translation': 'base_ensembl_translation'})

Form to the node type of its ids without version (gene -> base_ensembl_gene).

BASE_GENE = 'base_ensembl_gene'

The node type of gene ids without version.

CONNECTION_KEY = 'connection'

The key of an edge’s cross-reference record among its attributes.

ENSEMBL_TYPE = mappingproxy({'gene': 'ensembl_gene', 'transcript': 'ensembl_transcript', 'translation': 'ensembl_translation'})

Form to the node type of its versioned ids (gene -> ensembl_gene).

EXTERNAL = 'external'

The node type of an identifier of an external database (a symbol, an accession, …).

FORMS: tuple[str, ...] = ('gene', 'transcript', 'translation')

Ensembl’s forms, in the order in which one leads to the next (a translation belongs to a transcript, which belongs to a gene).

FORM_OF_ENSEMBL_TYPE = mappingproxy({'ensembl_gene': 'gene', 'ensembl_transcript': 'transcript', 'ensembl_translation': 'translation'})

Node type of versioned ids to its form (ensembl_gene -> gene).

GENE = 'ensembl_gene'

The node type of versioned gene ids, the backbone.

ID_VERSION_DELIMITER = '.'

The character between an Ensembl stable id and its version (ENSG00000141510.18).

LRG_ID = re.compile('^LRG_\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?$')

An LRG record’s id, with or without version.

NODE_TYPE_KEY = 'node_type'

The key of a node’s type among its attributes.

NUMBERED_SUFFIX = re.compile('^(.+)([\\-_\\.])([0-9]+)$')

(string before, separator, digits).

Type:

A string that ends in one of the SEPARATORS and digits

RETIRED = 'Retired'

The version of the node after the last version of a gene id (its retirement).

SENTINEL_VERSIONS: frozenset[str] = frozenset({'Retired', 'Void'})

versions that no release holds.

Type:

Both marks

SEPARATORS = '-_.'

the step "separator" of the name resolution reads them as one (decision 87). A version (NM_000546.6, ENSG00000141510.18) follows one of them, and so does the number a single-cell tool appends to a repeated name (SRF.1, SRF-1, SRF_1: decision 82).

Type:

The characters that join the parts of a name (MIR138-2, H1_0, NKX2.1)

STABLE_ID = re.compile('(?i)^(?:ENS[A-Z]*\\d{11}|LRG_\\d+)$', re.IGNORECASE)

An Ensembl stable id or an LRG id without version, in any letter case (STABLE_ID_FORM).

STABLE_ID_FORM = '(?:ENS[A-Z]*\\d{11}|LRG_\\d+)'

ENS, the species’ letters and the letter of the feature, then eleven digits (ENSG00000141510, ENSMUST00000000001), or an LRG record’s id (LRG_<number>). A pattern to embed (no anchors, no flags).

Type:

The form of an Ensembl stable id without its version, by Ensembl’s scheme of identifiers

SYNONYM_PREFIX = 'synonym_id::'

the graph’s bookkeeping, never part of an id.

Type:

The prefix of the graph’s synonym nodes (synonym_id::TP53)

VOID = 'Void'

The version of the node before the first version of a gene id (its birth).

How an identifier is read

How an identifier a user typed or pasted is read before it is looked up in a graph.

What people paste carries more than the identifier: white space, invisible characters (a byte-order mark at the start of a file, zero-width spaces, bidirectional marks, soft hyphens, control characters), full-width letters and Unicode dashes, quotation marks and the punctuation that ends a sentence or an item of a list (A1BG;, CCDC39.), the placeholder of a missing value (nan, NA), and sometimes the form GENCODE gives the Y copies of the genes and transcripts of the pseudoautosomal regions (ENSG00000182378.14_PAR_Y).

Characters are classed by the Unicode standard (unicodedata): by their general category where one says what they are, and, where the standard defines the class by a property that unicodedata does not expose, by the few members of that property that remain after NFKC (each such constant below says so). read_identifier() is the one place that turns such a string into the text that is looked up, and says what it changed, so that a conversion reports it (idtrack.results.ConversionResult.match, whose prefixes unicode, punctuation and par_y idtrack.results.MATCH_PREFIXES describes).

Every rule here is a rule of the string alone, the same in every graph. This module imports nothing of idtrack except idtrack.errors and idtrack.ids.

MAX_ENSEMBL_VERSION = 65535

Ensembl’s core schema stores a version as SMALLINT UNSIGNED (16 bits).

Type:

The largest version of an Ensembl id

MAX_IDENTIFIER_LENGTH = 1000

The longest identifier that is read (after surrounding white space is removed). A bound on the work a string can cause, not a rule of identifiers: it is set where it is read, before any graph is consulted, so that one string gets one answer in every graph; the longest name in the graphs of the five organisms of idtrack’s table has about a hundred characters, and every bound above that gives the same answers.

MAX_VERSION_DIGITS = 5

The most digits a version of an Ensembl id can have (MAX_ENSEMBL_VERSION).

MISSING_VALUES: frozenset[str] = frozenset({'#n/a', '#n/a n/a', '#na', '-1.#ind', '-1.#qnan', '-nan', '1.#ind', '1.#qnan', '<na>', 'n/a', 'na', 'nan', 'nat', 'none', 'null', 'unknown'})

pandas’ missing values (PANDAS_MISSING_VALUES) and the two that decision 81 adds, pandas’ text of a missing date or time (NaT) and UniProt’s placeholder name (unknown). They stand for nothing far more often than for a gene (NaN is an old alias of SCN11A, NA a synonym of a few genes); a caller who names the source database (from_database) has them looked up as identifiers of that database.

Type:

The spellings of a missing value, compared without letter case after the reading below

PANDAS_MISSING_VALUES: frozenset[str] = frozenset({'', '#N/A', '#N/A N/A', '#NA', '-1.#IND', '-1.#QNAN', '-NaN', '-nan', '1.#IND', '1.#QNAN', '<NA>', 'N/A', 'NA', 'NULL', 'NaN', 'None', 'n/a', 'nan', 'null'})

The strings that pandas reads as a missing value by default (pandas._libs.parsers.STR_NA_VALUES of pandas 3.1): the lists and tables people paste are mostly written by pandas or read with it (decision 52). Copied here, not read, because the query path imports no pandas (it needs numpy and networkx only); a unit test compares the copy with pandas’ own list, so that a change of the source fails a test instead of drifting.

read_identifier(value, argument='identifier', from_database=None)[source]

Read an identifier as idtrack looks it up, or refuse it.

In this order: surrounding white space is removed; the string is refused when it is empty, longer than MAX_IDENTIFIER_LENGTH, a spelling of a missing value (unless from_database is named) or one of the graph’s internal names; Unicode is normalised (normalise_unicode(), kind "unicode"); quotes around it and stray punctuation at its end are removed (strip_punctuation(), kind "punctuation"); GENCODE’s <id>_PAR_Y is read as <id> (kind "par_y"). The checks of a missing value and of an internal name see the string after the Unicode and punctuation readings too ('NA' in quotes is NA).

Parameters:

  • value (Any) – The identifier given.

  • argument (str) – The name of the argument, for the error message.

  • from_database (str | None) – The database the caller names as the identifier’s source (None: none).

Returns:

The text to look up and what the reading changed.

Return type:

Reading

Raises:

  • ArgumentTypeError – If the value is not a string.

  • MissingValueError – If it is empty or a spelling of a missing value (and no source database is named).

  • InvalidArgumentError – If it is longer than any identifier, or one of the graph’s internal names.

strip_punctuation(text)[source]

Return a string without the quotation marks around it and the punctuation that ends a sentence at its end.

Repeatedly: the characters of Unicode’s Terminal_Punctuation at the end (;, ,, ., :, !, ?), and a pair of quotation marks that encloses the string ('AGT', “TP53”). A quotation mark at one end only stays (HSP70B' is a name), as does punctuation inside a string.

Parameters:

text (str) – The string.

Returns:

The string as it is matched; the string itself when nothing changes (or nothing would be left).

Return type:

str

class Place(assembly, region, start, end, strand, releases, kind='scaffold')[source]

Bases: NamedTuple

Where a gene lies: on an assembly, a sequence region, from start to end (1-based, inclusive), on a strand.

The fields: assembly, the key of the assembly (idtrack.organisms.ORGANISM_TABLE); region, the name of the sequence region (a chromosome, a scaffold, a patch); start and end, the first and last base of the gene as Ensembl counts them; strand, 1 or -1; releases, the releases at which the gene lies there on the assembly that serves the release; kind, what Ensembl’s tables say the sequence region is, one of idtrack.graph.genes.PLACE_KINDS (a chromosome, the mitochondrial genome, or a scaffold or another sequence below a chromosome; "scaffold" where the graph does not say). Whether two places overlap, and so whether two genes lie at one place, is the rule of idtrack.graph.genes.overlap(); the kind lets two places on different assemblies be compared (idtrack.graph.genes.relation()).

class ReleaseSet[source]

Bases: frozenset

An immutable set of Ensembl releases with its bit mask, one object per distinct value.

It is a frozenset (membership, iteration, |, &, min, max and comparison with any set work as usual) that also carries mask, an int whose bit r is set when release r is in the set, so that mask >> r & 1 tests membership and |/& on masks combine sets without building them. Equal sets are the same object: a graph with millions of edges holds a few thousand of them.

class TheGraph(*args, backend=None, **kwargs)[source]

Bases: NameResolution, MultiDiGraph

The identifier graph of one organism: Ensembl gene history plus cross-references, with typed accessors.

Nodes are identifiers: versioned Ensembl genes (the backbone, with <id>.Void and <id>.Retired marking births and retirements), versionless base gene ids, transcripts, translations and identifiers of external databases. Two families of edges exist. History edges connect backbone genes and carry the release pair of the event and Ensembl’s mapping score. Cross-reference edges (external id to Ensembl id, base id to versioned gene, transcript to gene, translation to transcript) carry a Connection: the releases in which each database links the two nodes on each assembly.

The class is built by idtrack.GraphMaker and read by idtrack.engine.Track. A graph has two states. While it is being made it is an ordinary networkx.MultiDiGraph. freeze() (called by the first use of any accessor) turns the content into compact arrays: node names and types, edge arrays, and a small table of distinct connections whose release sets are bit masks. A frozen graph cannot be changed, is what save() writes and load() reads back in seconds without network access, and answers every question per node on demand behind bounded caches, so that nothing derived from the graph can be stale and no table over all nodes is kept in memory.

The networkx reading interface (g.nodes[n], g.neighbors(n), g.get_edge_data(u, v), g[u][v][k]) keeps working on a frozen graph; the accessors of this class (history_edges(), xref_edges(), active_ranges(), combined(), resolve_name() …) are the faster way to read it.

Create an empty, mutable graph; arguments are those of networkx.MultiDiGraph.

Parameters:

  • args (Any) – Positional arguments accepted by networkx.MultiDiGraph.__init__().

  • kwargs (Any) – Keyword arguments accepted by networkx.MultiDiGraph.__init__(); they become graph attributes (organism, assembly, confident_for_release …) of a graph made in memory; a built or loaded graph has its record instead.

A database that gives no version (a symbol, an NCBI gene id) has none here.

Parameters:

Return type:

Return the release ranges in which a node exists: [[first, last], ...], inclusive and ascending.

For a backbone gene the ranges come from its history edges: a range starts at the new_release of an edge that enters the node and ends at the old_release of the last edge that leaves it; the last range of an id that is alive at the last release of the graph ends at infinity. For every other node the ranges are the releases of its cross-reference edges, whatever the database and assembly.

The ranges. Do not change the list (it is cached).

  • KeyError – If a node that is not a backbone gene has no cross-reference edge.

Nothing per node is precomputed: the per-node values (combined(), active_ranges(), trios()) are computed when asked for and kept in bounded caches. Return a gene’s places on the reference sequence carried onto later assemblies by Ensembl’s mapping (decision 103).

Where Ensembl publishes a mapping of an earlier assembly of the organism onto a later one (its chain files, idtrack.build.assembly_chain), the builder carries every place of a version on the reference sequence of the earlier assembly onto each later one, by its aligned bases: one place per region and strand of the later assembly that holds some of them, from the first to the last base carried there. A place that no aligned base carries has none. The places are compared with those of the later assembly by overlap, as places on one assembly are (idtrack.graph.genes.relation()).

copy(as_view=False)

Returns a copy of the graph.

The copy method by default returns an independent shallow copy of the graph and attributes. That is, if an attribute is a container, that container is shared by the original an the copy. Use Python’s copy.deepcopy for new containers.

If as_view is True then a view is returned instead of a copy.

Notes

All copies reproduce the graph structure, but data attributes may be handled in different ways. There are four types of copies of a graph that people might want.

Deepcopy – A “deepcopy” copies the graph structure as well as all data attributes and any objects they might contain. The entire graph object is new so that changes in the copy do not affect the original object. (see Python’s copy.deepcopy)

Data Reference (Shallow) – For a shallow copy the graph structure is copied but the edge, node and graph attribute dicts are references to those in the original graph. This saves time and memory but could cause confusion if you change an attribute in one graph and it changes the attribute in the other. NetworkX does not provide this level of shallow copy.

Independent Shallow – This copy creates new independent attribute dicts and then does a shallow copy of the attributes. That is, any attributes that are containers are shared between the new graph and the original. This is exactly what dict.copy() provides. You can obtain this style copy using:

>>> G = nx.path_graph(5)
>>> H = G.copy()
>>> H = G.copy(as_view=False)
>>> H = nx.Graph(G)
>>> H = G.__class__(G)

Fresh Data – For fresh data, the graph structure is copied while new empty data attribute dicts are created. The resulting graph is independent of the original and it has no edge, node or graph attributes. Fresh copies are not enabled. Instead use:

>>> H = G.__class__()
>>> H.add_nodes_from(G)
>>> H.add_edges_from(G.edges)

View – Inspired by dict-views, graph-views act like read-only versions of the original graph, providing a copy of the original structure without requiring any memory for copying the information.

See the Python copy module for more information on shallow and deep copies, https://docs.python.org/3/library/copy.html.

Parameters:

as_view (bool, optional (default=False)) – If True, the returned graph-view provides a read-only view of the original graph without actually copying any data.

Returns:

G – A copy of the graph.

Return type:

Graph

See also

to_directed

return a directed copy of the graph.

Examples

>>> G = nx.path_graph(4)  # or DiGraph, MultiGraph, MultiDiGraph, etc
>>> H = G.copy()
count_genes(stable_ids, release=None)[source]

Return how many genes some stable gene ids name (the one rule: idtrack.graph.genes.count_genes()).

The ids are compared where the graph tells loci apart, in frames: at one release (ids that live then are one gene only where their places overlap then), on one assembly (ids whose places overlap, or that Ensembl’s history carried one to the other where they follow one another, are one gene) and by the names of chromosomes across assemblies (places(), their kinds). The count is the size of a set of ids told pairwise apart by some frame: one id of each locus of the frame that shows the most loci, extended by every id told apart from each id of the set so far, so that the evidence of several frames adds up. A copy that lies only outside the reference sequence (non_reference_releases()) adds no gene. Ids that nothing tells apart are one gene. A graph made in memory holds no places: an id lives at the releases of its history (active_releases()), and ids that live at one release are two genes.

Parameters:

  • stable_ids (Collection[str]) – Stable gene ids, without version.

  • release (int | None) – Count at this release only: the loci of the ids that live at it and lie on the reference sequence there (an id that does not live at it adds none).

Returns:

The number of genes (0 for no id, at least 1 for some).

Return type:

int

display_links(node, gene)

Return the databases whose link of an external identifier to a gene is the gene’s display name, with releases.

Ensembl’s display name of a gene is one cross reference (gene.display_xref_id), of one database, spelt as that database writes it (spelling() of the link). A graph that does not keep the database of its display names gives them under "" (the spelling is then not known).

Parameters:

  • node (str) – An external node.

  • gene (str) – A gene id with version.

Returns:

{database: release bit mask}; empty where the identifier never is the gene’s display name.

Return type:

dict[str, int]

display_rank(node, gene, release, typed)

Rank how a typed string is a gene’s display name at a release (decision 102; idtrack.engine.ranking).

The display name holds for the spelling typed. Letter case is evidence only where the string has letters of both cases: then the gene’s display name is the string only where its database spelt it so at the release (mouse Foxl1 at 70 is the display name of the gene MGI names so, not of the gene UniProt displays as FOXL1); separators are not compared (the step "separator" reads them as one). A string in one letter case carries no evidence of case (decisions 55 and 80): it is read without case, and in an organism whose symbols are written in mixed case (symbol_case()) the display name of a name authority (authority_databases) ranks before another source’s (mouse GAPDH is the gene MGI displays as Gapdh before the gene UniProt displays as GAPDH).

Parameters:

  • node (str) – The external node the string was read as.

  • gene (str) – A gene id with version.

  • release (int) – The release the string is read at.

  • typed (str) – The string as typed (without a version written after an accession).

Returns:

0 the display name; 1 another source’s display name, for a string in one letter case where symbols are written in mixed case; 2 not the gene’s display name there.

Return type:

int

display_releases(node, gene)

Return the releases at which an external identifier is a gene’s display name (gene.display_xref_id).

Ensembl gives every gene at every release one display name, whatever database it came from (an authority’s symbol, a projection of another organism’s, NCBI’s, UniProt’s): Ensembl’s own statement of the gene’s name there. It ranks a gene first among the genes that carry a name at one release (idtrack.engine.ranking).

Parameters:

The release bit mask, on the assembly that serves each release; 0 where it never is.

freeze()[source]

Turn the graph into its compact, read-only form (idempotent).

Node names, node types and edges are moved into arrays, release sets become interned ReleaseSet objects inside interned Connection objects, and the networkx dictionaries are replaced by read-only views over the arrays. From then on the graph cannot be changed and all accessors and derived values are available.

The graph itself.

TheGraph

ValueError – If node names are not strings or edge keys are not integers.

genes_linked_at_once(node)[source]

Return the largest number of different genes that a node is linked to in a single release.

Genes are counted by stable id, whatever their versions; a transcript or a translation counts as its gene. For an external identifier this says how specific it is: 1 for an id of one gene, however many versions of that gene it was linked to over the years, and hundreds for the name of a gene family. A gene’s copies outside the reference sequence count here (unlike count_genes()): an id that a gene shares with many copies at once (the genes of the human MHC on its haplotypes) stays no bridge, which is what Ensembl’s history gives for an id retired without a successor (counted by count_genes(), such ids bridged retired copies to other copies: seven human lines of the truth file of the tests became wrong).

Parameters:

node (str) – A node with outgoing cross-reference edges (an external identifier).

Returns:

The largest number of gene stable ids linked in one release; 0 if the node links no gene.

Return type:

int

This is name resolution per database and release, as data: the caller decides which databases count (a symbol database, a database of names, synonyms) and at which release. A name counts at a release only on the assembly that serves that release, and only for a gene of the reference sequence there; a name a database recorded as a synonym of the gene is marked idtrack.results.NameMatch.synonym.

Parameters:

  • name (str) – The name, as written (surrounding white space is part of it).

  • fold_case (bool) – Match without letter case; otherwise the name must be written as the database wrote it at the release (a database may write a name in another case at another release).

Returns:

One record per (name, gene, database) with the releases at which it holds, sorted by database, gene and name; empty when the name names no gene.

Return type:

list[NameMatch]

Raises:

  • ArgumentTypeError – If name is not a string.

  • InvalidArgumentError – If name begins with the graph’s internal prefix of synonyms (decision 56).

Return the release ranges in which a gene exists on any assembly.

active_ranges() of a backbone gene describes the backbone: each release as the organism’s preferred assembly of that release has it. A gene can also exist at a release on another assembly (human GRCh37 keeps its genes in every release after GRCh38 took over). This method adds those releases. It also checks the two sources against each other: the releases in which the gene is referred to on the assembly that serves the backbone at that release must lie inside the backbone ranges.

Raises:

  • UnknownIdentifierError – If the node is not a backbone gene.

get_edge_data(u, v, key=None, default=None)

Returns the attribute dictionary associated with edge (u, v, key).

If a key is not provided, returns a dictionary mapping edge keys to attribute dictionaries for each edge between u and v.

This is identical to G[u][v][key] except the default is returned instead of an exception is the edge doesn’t exist.

Parameters:

  • u (nodes)

  • v (nodes)

  • default (any Python object (default=None)) – Value to return if the specific edge (u, v, key) is not found, OR if there are no edges between u and v and no key is specified.

  • key (hashable identifier, optional (default=None)) – Return data only for the edge with specified key, as an attribute dictionary (rather than a dictionary mapping keys to attribute dictionaries).

Returns:

edge_dict – The edge attribute dictionary, OR a dictionary mapping edge keys to attribute dictionaries for each of those edges if no specific key is provided (even if there’s only one edge between u and v).

Return type:

dictionary

Examples

>>> G = nx.MultiGraph()  # or MultiDiGraph
>>> key = G.add_edge(0, 1, key="a", weight=7)
>>> G[0][1]["a"]  # key='a'
{'weight': 7}
>>> G.edges[0, 1, "a"]  # key='a'
{'weight': 7}

Warning: we protect the graph data structure by making G.edges and G[1][2] read-only dict-like structures. However, you can assign values to attributes in e.g. G.edges[1, 2, ‘a’] or G[1][2][‘a’] using an additional bracket as shown next. You need to specify all edge info to assign to the edge data associated with an edge.

>>> G[0][1]["a"]["weight"] = 10
>>> G.edges[0, 1, "a"]["weight"] = 10
>>> G[0][1]["a"]["weight"]
10
>>> G.edges[1, 0, "a"]["weight"]
10

>>> G = nx.MultiGraph()  # or MultiDiGraph
>>> nx.add_path(G, [0, 1, 2, 3])
>>> G.edges[0, 1, 0]["weight"] = 5
>>> G.get_edge_data(0, 1)
{0: {'weight': 5}}
>>> e = (0, 1)
>>> G.get_edge_data(*e)  # tuple form
{0: {'weight': 5}}
>>> G.get_edge_data(3, 0)  # edge not in graph, returns None
>>> G.get_edge_data(3, 0, default=0)  # edge not in graph, return default
0
>>> G.get_edge_data(1, 0, 0)  # specific key gives back
{'weight': 5}

has_edge(u, v, key=None)

Returns True if the graph has an edge between nodes u and v.

This is the same as v in G[u] or key in G[u][v] without KeyError exceptions.

Parameters:

  • u (nodes) – Nodes can be, for example, strings or numbers.

  • v (nodes) – Nodes can be, for example, strings or numbers.

  • key (hashable identifier, optional (default=None)) – If specified return True only if the edge with key is found.

Returns:

edge_ind – True if edge is in the graph, False otherwise.

Return type:

bool

Examples

Can be called either using two nodes u, v, an edge tuple (u, v), or an edge tuple (u, v, key).

>>> G = nx.MultiGraph()  # or MultiDiGraph
>>> nx.add_path(G, [0, 1, 2, 3])
>>> G.has_edge(0, 1)  # using two nodes
True
>>> e = (0, 1)
>>> G.has_edge(*e)  #  e is a 2-tuple (u, v)
True
>>> G.add_edge(0, 1, key="a")
'a'
>>> G.has_edge(0, 1, key="a")  # specify key
True
>>> G.has_edge(1, 0, key="a")  # edges aren't directed
True
>>> e = (0, 1, "a")
>>> G.has_edge(*e)  # e is a 3-tuple (u, v, 'a')
True

The following syntax are equivalent:

>>> G.has_edge(0, 1)
True
>>> 1 in G[0]  # though this gives :exc:`KeyError` if 0 not in G
True
>>> 0 in G[1]  # other order; also gives :exc:`KeyError` if 0 not in G
True

property hyperconnective_nodes: dict[str, int]

External identifiers that more genes share than an identity can, with that number of genes.

An external id is hyper-connective when, in a single Ensembl release, it is linked to more than idtrack.settings.GraphSettings.hyperconnective_threshold different genes (genes_linked_at_once(): genes by stable id, whatever their versions; a transcript or a translation counts as its gene). Such ids are names of gene families and accessions shared by paralogues (RFAM families, U6, 5S_rRNA, snoRNA names): they say what kind of gene something is, not which gene. Following them in a synonym search multiplies the candidates and bridges unrelated genes, so the search does not follow them. A label (an id of one of label_databases: a display name, a symbol) is a family name too when it named more genes than that over all its releases (label_families, genes as count_genes() counts them: the ids of one locus over the releases are one gene, a copy outside the reference sequence adds none): Ensembl gives a snoRNA’s family name to the copy it names at each release, a few at a time (mouse SCARNA15: 9 genes over the releases, at most 5 at once), and such a name carried a retired id to copies at other loci.

The count at once is per release, so the set does not grow with the number of releases in the graph: an id linked to many successive versions of one gene, or to a few genes that change over the years, is not hyper-connective, however many edges it has. The threshold was chosen by measurement against Ensembl’s own data (pig: with 5, no kind of query is answered worse and 15 kinds better than with the earlier rule, more than 20 edges over all releases; with 10 or 20 the family ids shared by 6 to 20 genes become bridges and conversions of retired ids get worse). It is the threshold of the graph’s settings (idtrack.TheGraph.graph_settings, given when a graph is loaded), read whenever this property is read, so another threshold needs no graph built again: load the file with other settings. Counting by stable id counts a gene’s copies on alternative loci and patches as genes here (unlike label_families), on purpose (genes_linked_at_once() says why).

Returns:

{external node: number of genes} for the hyper-connective nodes: the largest number of genes linked in one release, or, for a label that is a family name over its releases only, the number of genes it named over them.

Return type:

dict[str, int]

non_reference_releases(node)[source]

Return the releases at which a gene lies outside the reference sequence of its genome assembly.

Ensembl annotates genes on the chromosomes and scaffolds of an assembly (the reference sequence) and on regions beside it: alternative loci (haplotypes), assembly patches and LRG records. A gene on such a region is a copy of, or an alternative to, a gene of the reference sequence, with a stable id of its own. The builder takes the fact from Ensembl’s core database of every release, for the assembly that serves the release in the backbone (serving_assembly): the sequence region of the gene carries the attribute idtrack.build.database_manager.NON_REFERENCE_ATTRIBUTE.

Parameters:

node (str) – A node of the graph.

Returns:

The releases; empty for a gene of the reference sequence, for a node that is not a gene of the backbone, and for every node of a graph that was made in memory rather than built.

Return type:

ReleaseSet

Raises:

UnknownIdentifierError – If the node is not in the graph.

number_of_edges(u=None, v=None)

Returns the number of edges between two nodes.

Parameters:

  • u (nodes, optional (Default=all edges)) – If u and v are specified, return the number of edges between u and v. Otherwise return the total number of all edges.

  • v (nodes, optional (Default=all edges)) – If u and v are specified, return the number of edges between u and v. Otherwise return the total number of all edges.

Returns:

nedges – The number of edges in the graph. If nodes u and v are specified return the number of edges between those nodes. If the graph is directed, this only returns the number of edges from u to v.

Return type:

int

See also

size

Examples

For undirected multigraphs, this method counts the total number of edges in the graph:

>>> G = nx.MultiGraph()
>>> G.add_edges_from([(0, 1), (0, 1), (1, 2)])
[0, 1, 0]
>>> G.number_of_edges()
3

If you specify two nodes, this counts the total number of edges joining the two nodes:

>>> G.number_of_edges(0, 1)
2

For directed multigraphs, this method can count the total number of directed edges from u to v:

>>> G = nx.MultiDiGraph()
>>> G.add_edges_from([(0, 1), (0, 1), (1, 0)])
[0, 1, 0]
>>> G.number_of_edges(0, 1)
2
>>> G.number_of_edges(1, 0)
1

readings(identifier, from_release=None, from_database=None, to_release=None)

Return every reading of a string that resolve_name() took, and those its rules set aside.

resolve_name() returns the first reading taken. Two rules take a reading before the order of the steps would, and the reading the steps would have taken is then set aside, so that a caller can report it:

  • Symbols without letter case first (decisions 55 and 80). In an organism whose symbol databases write symbols in mixed case (symbol_case(), read from the graph: MGI writes Trp53), a string in one letter case (AR, nos2) that is not exactly a name of the release is read first as a symbol of the organism’s symbol databases without letter case; where that names exactly one gene at the release, it is the reading taken (match "case"), and the reading of the steps (an exact synonym of another gene, AR of three) is set aside. A named from_database that is not a symbol database of the organism turns the rule off.

  • No separator variant joins a make-unique suffix into another gene’s synonym (decision 82). A string that ends in -<digits>, .<digits> or _<digits> (SRF.1: single-cell tools append such suffixes to repeated names) is not read by the steps "separator" and "case" as a synonym whose genes at the release are none of the genes to which a name authority gives the string before the suffix, written exactly so, as its symbol there (SRF-1, a synonym of SPATA6, while SRF is SRF’s HGNC symbol); that reading is set aside. A name reached so is read (MIR138_2 for the gene MIR138-2, H1_0 for H1-0: numbered names are written with these separators too).

A version is read where some database has it. Where the identifier before .<digits> is, at the release read, also an id of a database that gives it no version (accession_versions(): an NCBI gene id 2633 beside a numeric Havana translation id 2633 with version 1 at releases 50 and 51) and no link attaches it with that version at that release, the version reading is taken by the rules below and the identifier as that other database’s id is set aside beside it ("unversioned_database"): never one reading silently.

A step that finds several identifiers that exist at the release takes them all (decision 87: a separator reading that reaches several names is a tie, AY172335_1 for AY172335-1 and AY172335.1 where both are names at the release read). Readings are joined only where they exist at one release: when none exists at the release asked about, the string is read at the latest release at which one does (resolve_name()), and the readings of that release are taken (AY172335-1 is a name at releases 54 to 56 only and AY172335.1 at 57 to 60 only: without a release, AY172335_1 is read at 60, as AY172335.1).

A reading the steps reached before the one taken that exists only at other releases is reported with those releases (Readings.other_releases): a name of one gene then, read as a synonym of another gene at the release asked about, says what the string meant at another time (decision 99: the release asked about decides; ask at the other release for the other meaning).

Parameters:

  • identifier (str) – The string.

  • from_release (SupportsIndex | None) – As resolve_name().

  • from_database (str | None) – As resolve_name().

  • to_release (SupportsIndex | None) – As resolve_name().

Returns:

The readings taken (empty when the string means nothing) and those set aside.

Return type:

Readings

Raises:

  • ArgumentTypeError – As resolve_name().

  • InvalidArgumentError – If the string is an Ensembl id with a version longer than any Ensembl version.

resolve_name(identifier, from_release=None, from_database=None, to_release=None)

Find the node a user’s string means at a release, and say how it was matched.

This is the one place that says what a typed string means; the engine, the API, the inference of the source of a list and the self-tests all ask it, each naming the release it means.

Two things decide, in this order:

Existence at the release the question is about. Between the nodes the string can mean, one that exists at from_release (without one: at to_release, the release a conversion reads it at when it exists there; without either, the last release of the graph) is taken before one that does not. One release decides both which node the string means and where a conversion reads it. Databases reuse strings: slit2 was a synonym of one gene years ago and is, in another letter case, the name of another gene today; APC10 was the name of one gene and is a synonym of another today. Which of the two is meant depends on the release asked about, not on how the string happens to be spelt. An Ensembl stable id (of a gene, with or without version, a transcript or a translation) is never passed over for an external identifier or synonym spelt the same, at whatever release it exists: it is an id of Ensembl’s own history, which the graph follows through the releases. An external identifier exists at a release where a database has it on the genome assembly that serves the release (serving_line), as the engine counts a link: what an earlier assembly that Ensembl keeps listing beside the primary one says at such a release (human GRCh37, with its names of release 75 at every later release) does not make an identifier exist there, so a name that GRCh38 gave up and that is a synonym of a gene today is that synonym today. An identifier that only such an assembly ever has exists at no release and is still found (below). When the caller says which external database the string is an id of (from_database), “exists” means “is an id of that database at the release”, and among the nodes that are not, one that is an id of that database at some release comes before one that never is. The synonyms a database records are read under its name too, after all its names (every step on the names first): a string that the database gives no gene as a name at any release is read as one of its synonyms.

The steps, among the nodes that are equal in existence. They are tried in this order, each only if the one before found nothing. Each of the first four is tried on the names of the graph and then on its synonyms (the synonym node of the string, synonym_id::<string>; the match is then reported as "synonym:<step>") before the next step begins, so that a string that is exactly a synonym of one gene is that synonym, not a spelling variant of another gene’s name (H3.3B, a synonym, is not the name H3-3b):

  1. "exact": the string is an identifier exactly as it is written. For an Ensembl id that is the name of its node. For an external identifier it is how a link of it (to an Ensembl id, in a database: the one named, when from_database is given) writes it at the release the string is read at (above; for an identifier that does not exist there, at its latest release). Databases change the letter case of a name over the releases, two databases may write one name in two ways at one release, and one database may give two genes one name in two cases (Tc and tc); the graph keeps one node per identifier, named as at its last release, and how each link wrote it at each release (spelling()). So PRR2, typed for a release at which a database wrote the name so, is that name exactly, although the node is called prr2 after today’s spelling, and it is not taken for another gene’s synonym PRR2; typed prr2 for that release it is the same name by letter case. A conversion that matched a string exactly follows only the links spelt as typed (idtrack.engine.Track.convert()).

  2. "case": it is a node name when letter case is ignored.

  3. "separator": it is a node name when -, _ and . are taken as the same character (and case is ignored): HLA_A and HLA.A for HLA-A. An Ensembl id’s version is read only after ., as Ensembl writes it: ENSG00000123456_2 and ENSG00000123456-2 are not ENSG00000123456.2 (single-cell tools append such suffixes to make repeated names unique), and stay not found.

  4. "version": the string ends in .<digits> and the identifier without that suffix is a versioned accession (a link of it attaches a version, xref.version of Ensembl’s cross references: RefSeq, UniProt, CCDS, the EMBL protein ids; accession_versions()) and no id of a symbol database of the organism (idtrack.organisms.SYMBOL_DATABASES), and some link attached that version: NM_000546.5 for NM_000546 as the links that attached version 5 carry it, at the releases at which they did (decision 14’s rule for Ensembl ids, applied to accessions). Where the accession’s numbers come only from databases whose number is an edit counter of their records (edit_counter_databases(): UniProt’s entry version), the version is not judged: the accession is read without it, as "version_not_judged" (decision 101). Nothing else is ever cut off the name of an external identifier: SLA.7 and SLA_11 are not SLA, NM_713028147 is not NM.

  5. "version_newer_than_graph": the string is an Ensembl id with a version higher than every version the graph holds of it (written with .), and the id is active at the last release of the graph: the version may belong to a release newer than the graph, so the string stands for the latest version the graph holds, ENSG00000123456.99 for ENSG00000123456.7; or a versioned accession written with a version higher than every version its links attached (the step "version"), where a link of it holds at the last release of the graph (it can then be newer than the graph), read as the latest of them, as the links that attached it carry it. Any other version that the graph does not hold (a lower one, one in a gap, any version of a retired id; of an accession, one its links never attached, and one above all of an accession no link attaches at the last release) matches nothing; known_versions() then names the versions that exist. Where the identifier before the version is, at the release read, also an id of a database that gives it no version (an NCBI gene id spelt like a numeric Havana id), and no link has it with that version there, the string has two readings: the version reading (taken where it exists, by the rule below) and that database’s id, reported (readings(), "unversioned_database").

When no node the string can mean exists at the release, the string is read at the latest release at which one of them exists (with from_database: as an id of that database), by the steps and rules of that release, so that what it means and where it is read are again one release; the caller learns from the node where it does exist (Readings.here is False). A node that exists at no release on the assemblies that serve the graph’s releases (or, with from_database, is no id of that database at all) is taken, first in the order of the steps, only when no other node exists anywhere. The cost is a few dictionary look-ups, whatever the string.

Parameters:

  • identifier (str) – The string to resolve.

  • from_release (SupportsIndex | None) – The Ensembl release the question is about (for a conversion: the release the identifier is read at). None means the last release of the graph. A release the graph does not have is one at which no external identifier exists.

  • from_database (str | None) – The external database the string is meant as an id of. None: any database.

  • to_release (SupportsIndex | None) – Only without from_release: the release a conversion goes to, at which the string is read (which node exists, and how it is spelt in the step "exact") when one of its readings exists there. None: the last release of the graph.

Returns:

The node name and how it was matched, or (None, None).

Return type:

tuple[str | None, str | None]

Raises:

ArgumentTypeError – If identifier is not a string, or from_release or to_release is not an integer.

The view shares the arrays and the per-node caches of the graph; rev.neighbors(n) are the predecessors of n. The typed accessors of the view (history_edges(), xref_edges()) are reversed as well; everything that describes a node (active_ranges(), combined() …) is that of the graph itself.

save(path)[source]

Write the graph to a file, atomically.

The file is a NumPy .npz archive, deflated (no pickled objects): the node names, node types, edge arrays, the table of distinct connections with their release bit masks, the genes outside the reference sequence with their releases, the name indices, the spellings of the external ids, the places of the genes and those carried onto later assemblies (carried_places()), Ensembl’s assembly exceptions (assembly_exceptions), the versions of the accessions per link and release and the display names of the genes per release with the database each is filed under (accession_versions(), display_releases()), and one JSON document with the graph’s record and the tables computed from the content when it was built (the external ids that several genes share, the label families). It is written to a temporary file in the same folder and renamed, so an interrupted run leaves either the previous file or none, never a part of one.

Parameters:

path (str) – File to write.

Raises:

None
